justice: The street allocates substantial space to trees and planting strips on both sides, giving all road users a greener and calmer environment rather than dedicating all space to cars.

A narrow pedestrian edge exists along the right side with curb definition, but the walking space is discontinuous and partly interrupted by dirt patches, reducing equal quality of access for pedestrians.
Multiple parked scooters and small vehicles along the corridor occupy edge space and may limit fair shared use of the street for walkers and riders.
The right-side building entrance includes a ramp with handrails, which improves accessibility for a broad range of users.
No visible tactile paving, marked crossing, or dedicated accessible guidance features are present, so barrier-free access is only partial.
safety: The roadway is relatively narrow and appears to function as a low-speed internal residential street, which likely reduces severe vehicle conflict risk.
Dense trees and residential towers create clear enclosure and passive surveillance from surrounding buildings, supporting perceived personal safety in daytime.
Scooters and small vehicles parked along both sides create potential edge friction and unexpected movements into the travel lane.
There is no visible marked sidewalk separation on the left and no dedicated bike lane, so pedestrians and cyclists may need to mix with motorized users.
The straight corridor provides long sightlines ahead, helping users detect oncoming vehicles and obstacles.
livability: The abundant mature trees and waterside edge on the left create a pleasant residential setting with greenery and visual relief.
A bench area and informal sitting spot near the right-side planting bed support lingering and everyday neighborhood use.
High-rise residential buildings directly front the street, indicating a lived-in environment with nearby housing access.
The corridor lacks visible shops, active ground-floor uses, or community services, so daily activity diversity appears limited.
The street feels quiet and local rather than vibrant, which supports residential calm but lowers broader urban vitality.
sustainability: Large mature trees along the left side provide significant canopy cover, supporting shade, cooling, and urban ecological value.
The compact internal street layout within a residential area can shorten local trips and reduce dependence on higher-speed car travel.
Numerous two- and three-wheeled vehicles suggest some use of smaller, lower-space transport modes compared with full-sized cars.
Unpaved soil patches and limited visible permeable green infrastructure details suggest stormwater management is only basic.
No dedicated public transit stop or explicit cycling facility is visible, limiting stronger support for low-carbon mode shift.
aesthetics: The mature tree canopy creates a strong green visual frame and softens the street significantly.
The combination of waterside fencing, planting, and residential towers gives the scene depth and a relatively orderly composition.
Building facades are consistent in material and height, contributing to a coherent residential character.
Some parked scooters, bins, and bare soil patches reduce visual neatness at ground level.
Overall cleanliness is acceptable, and the street appears reasonably maintained without major litter or damage.
comfort: Extensive tree cover on the left and additional shrubs on the right improve thermal comfort by providing shade and cooling.
A bench and shaded sitting area near the right-side greenery offer a place to rest, improving physical comfort.
The internal residential street appears quiet with limited traffic, which likely lowers noise stress and improves psychological comfort.
Walking surfaces are mixed: the roadway is smooth, but parts of the pedestrian edge transition to dirt and uneven margins, reducing physical comfort.
The enclosed greenery and residential setting create a calmer atmosphere, though parked scooters can make movement feel slightly cluttered.
walkability: The street has a low-speed residential character and long forward visibility, which helps basic pedestrian movement.
Tree shade and greenery make walking more pleasant, especially in warm conditions.
A ramp with handrails at the building side supports access to the adjacent entrance zone.
There is no clearly continuous, wide sidewalk along the full corridor, especially on the left side where pedestrians would likely share space near the carriageway.
No marked crosswalks, pedestrian priority markings, or clear footpath separation are visible, limiting overall walkability.
bikeability: The low-speed, low-volume residential street may be rideable for confident cyclists because traffic appears relatively calm.
The corridor is straight and visually open, which helps riders anticipate oncoming vehicles.
There is no dedicated bike lane, painted cycle marking, or physical protection for cyclists.
Parked scooters and edge-side vehicles can create obstacles and dooring/conflict risk for people cycling.
No visible bicycle parking or cycling wayfinding is provided, so convenience for everyday cycling appears weak.
